newsitem.title: GREECE: Papandreou widow vexes friends, foes with TV grief.
newsitem.headline: Papandreou widow vexes friends, foes with TV grief.

text.p: A televised display of grief by Dimitra Liani, controversial widow of Socialist Party founder Andreas Papandreou, got brickbats from friends and foes alike on Wednesday.
Greeks accused her of an excessive bid for popular sympathy, three months after the death of her husband, a flamboyant ex-premier, touched off scenes of national mourning.
"Enough, Dimitra," cried a headline in the liberal Eleftherotypia, which called her television appearance "a show in bad taste unworthy of Papandreou's memory."
She cooperated in a programme aired on Monday and Tuesday night, billed as an exclusive report with close-ups and a tour of her home.
Liani made no immediate public comment on the storm of criticism, even from newspapers long tolerant toward the ex-Olympic Airways flight attendant whose romance with Papandreou divided many.
Liani, dressed in flowing black with a deep neckline accentuated by three strings of pearls, was seen praying and lighting white candles in the private chapel on the grounds of her pink villa.
She carefully bent her blonde head to kiss Byzantine icons to the sound of a Greek liturgy.

"I long for this unique relationship that marked both our lives and I hold on to all that was special, his presence here and memories and I dream of the moment when we meet again," she said as cameras scanned the home Papandreou built for her in an exclusive northern Athens suburb.

She met Papandreou in 1988 while serving him drinks on an airliner. He shocked the nation by flaunting his extramarital affair to the woman whose nude-bathing photographs were splashed in newspapers around the world.
The nation and the media watched their relationship with the intensity of a television soap-opera.
Pro-socialist newspapers exploded in anger over her latest display. "We supported her. We even tolerated her thirst for publicity," said the liberal Ethnos.
"But she has now crossed the line and her grace period is over. Those who saw her playing the grieving widow in expensive black outfits and pretending in front of the icons felt rage and disgust."
Papandreou divorced Margaret, his American wife of 37 years and mother of his four children, to marry Liani in 1989.
She stood by him through election defeats, scandals and heart surgery but she was branded an opportunist with political ambitions by many socialist politicians.
Liani's political hopes crashed after Papandreou, who ruled from 1981 to 1989 and won a third term in 1993, died last June. He was 77, 36 years older than Liani.
Papandreou left her his sole heir in a will replete with tender words, describing her as the great love of his life and asking his friends to support her after he was gone.
One of his closest friends and an ardent Liani supporter for years, former merchant marine minister George Katsifaras, was among those who denounced her latest show.
"These things should not be done in public," he said. "When you truly love someone you bear your suffering quietly and alone."
